n: Paul moved on to Corinth, a wealthy, busy port city known for its loose morals. He would later write at least two letters to the church he founded here.

f.g: Capital of the Roman province of Achaia (southern Greece), on a narrow isthmus between two seas.

n: There he met Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple recently expelled from Rome when Emperor Claudius banished the Jews (about AD 49). They became lifelong friends and co-workers.

f.w: Claudius had commanded all Jews to depart from Rome
f.g: The Roman historian Suetonius mentions this expulsion, linked to disturbances over “Chrestus.”

n: Paul shared their trade as a tentmaker or leatherworker, so he lived and worked with them. Paul often supported himself so he wouldn’t burden the people he taught.

f.g: Makers of tents, probably from leather or woven goat hair.

n: Every Sabbath he reasoned in the synagogue, trying to persuade both Jews and Greeks.
When Silas and Timothy arrived, likely bringing gifts from Macedonia, Paul could devote himself fully to preaching, testifying that Jesus is the Messiah.

f.g: Many manuscripts read “occupied with the word” — fully devoted to preaching.

n: When the synagogue opposed him, Paul shook out his clothes in protest, declaring himself free of responsibility for them, and turned to the Gentiles.

f.w: Your blood be upon your own heads

n: Paul moved his teaching to the home of Justus, a Gentile worshipper of God whose house was right next to the synagogue.
Crispus, the synagogue’s leader, believed with his whole family — a major conversion. Many Corinthians believed and were baptized.
The Lord spoke to Paul in a night vision: Don’t be afraid; keep speaking. Even Paul needed reassurance.
The Lord promised protection and said, “I have much people in this city” — many prepared hearts not yet found.

f.w: I have much people in this city

n: Paul stayed eighteen months in Corinth, teaching God’s word — one of his longest stays anywhere.
When Gallio became governor of Achaia (about AD 51), opponents brought Paul to court. An inscription found at Delphi dates Gallio’s term, helping scholars date Paul’s travels.

f.g: Brother of the philosopher Seneca; proconsul of Achaia about AD 51–52.
Greek bēma — the raised platform where officials heard cases.

n: They accused Paul of teaching worship that violated the law — hoping Rome would treat Christianity as an illegal religion.
Before Paul could defend himself, Gallio cut in: if this were a real crime, I would hear it.
But since this was a dispute about words, names, and Jewish law, Gallio refused to judge it. His ruling effectively let Christianity be treated as part of Judaism, a legal religion.
He dismissed them from his court.
The crowd then beat Sosthenes, the new synagogue leader, in front of the court, and Gallio ignored it. A Sosthenes later appears as Paul’s fellow believer — possibly the same man.
After more time, Paul sailed for Syria with Priscilla and Aquila. At Cenchrea, Corinth’s eastern port, he cut his hair to complete a vow — probably a Nazarite-style vow of devotion.

f.g: Corinth’s harbor on the Aegean side.

n: They reached Ephesus, where Priscilla and Aquila stayed. Paul reasoned briefly with the Jews in the synagogue.

f.g: Major city of the province of Asia, home of the great temple of Artemis (Diana).

n: The Ephesian Jews asked him to stay longer, but he declined.
He wanted to reach Jerusalem for an upcoming feast but promised to return “if God will” — a humble way to make plans.
He landed at Caesarea, went up to greet the church in Jerusalem, then returned to Antioch — ending his second missionary journey.

f.g: Gone up to Jerusalem, which sits high in the hills.

n: After a stay in Antioch, Paul set out again through Galatia and Phrygia, strengthening the disciples. This begins his third missionary journey.
Meanwhile Apollos came to Ephesus — a Jew from Alexandria in Egypt, a gifted speaker deeply versed in the scriptures.

f.g: Great Egyptian city and center of Jewish learning in Greek.

n: Apollos taught about Jesus with zeal and accuracy, but he knew only John’s baptism. His knowledge was sincere but incomplete.
Priscilla and Aquila heard him, took him aside privately, and explained God’s way more completely. A model of kind, discreet correction — and a woman taking part in teaching.

f.w: expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly

n: When Apollos decided to go to Greece, the Ephesian believers wrote a letter of recommendation. In Corinth he greatly helped the believers.
He powerfully refuted his opponents in public debate, proving from scripture that Jesus is the Christ.

f.w: shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ
